requests.request: To the NYC Open Data team, I run NeighbourhoodIQ (tentative, not yet made public), a web application showing a home buyer the public-record context of a single address — schools, hazards, local services, and the property's sale history. I would like to include New York City using the Department of Finance's Citywide Annualized Calendar Sales Update (w2pb-icbu), and would be grateful for a line confirming the Terms of Use permit it. I ask because the dataset sets no licence — neither license nor licenseId is populated — so what governs is a chain: NYC Open Data's terms say the user "agrees to all of the Terms of Use of NYC.gov", and those state that materials "contained in or displayed on NYC.gov … are the property of the City of New York. All rights are reserved." My reading is that the reserved-rights clause addresses the website rather than the datasets the City publishes for reuse. But that is my inference, and I would rather have it confirmed. Could you confirm whether the following is permitted: 1. Querying the API live, one property at a time, when a visitor looks up a specific address — no bulk download and no mirror. 2. Displaying, for that property, the sale date, price and building class, attributed to the New York City Department of Finance. 3. Doing so in a commercial product. The application is a commercial service, which is why I am asking rather than assuming. Two things I will state rather than leave you to ask: - No party names. This dataset carries none. And where the application already reads ACRIS, party names live in the separate Parties dataset (636b-3b5g), which it never queries — only Master (bnx9-e6tj) and Legals (8h5j-fqxa). - No implied qualification. This dataset has no deed type or arm's-length flag, so a $0 transfer is not distinguishable from a market sale. Where the record does not say, the application says it does not know rather than presenting a guess as a fact. One question for the Department of Finance, if it can be passed on: the Open Data copy updates annually and runs through December 2025, while the rolling sales files cover the most recent twelve months. Is there a machine-readable route to current-year data other than the rolling spreadsheets? Happy to follow any attribution wording or rate limit you prefer. Kind regards, *****
requests.response: There is no machine-readable route to current-year data other than the rolling spreadsheet. As for using this data in your product: per the Open Data Law (https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/open-data-law/), users do not need a license in order to copy, reuse, or share the data on NYC Open Data. New York City's open data is free for anyone to use for any purpose they see fit. We do not require, but encourage users to cite the data and share the results under a similarly permissive license. Our team would love to see the results of your analysis! Once they're done, please submit any project that uses NYC Open Data to be featured on our Project Gallery (https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/projects/) via this submission form: https://opendata.cityofnewyork.us/project-submit/.

requests.request: I am requesting a public NYC DOB Open Data dataset or API-accessible view that identifies legacy BIS electrical permits that are in Abandoned, Inactive, Location Problem, Objection, or other unresolved/problem status, and shows whether those permits have been reinstated, refiled, inspected, completed, administratively closed, or otherwise resolved through DOB NOW: Build. The question I am trying to answer is: For each legacy BIS electrical permit that appears abandoned or unresolved, has that permit been resolved through DOB NOW: Build, and if so, what DOB NOW job/filing number, inspection result, Pass-Final date, Complete date, or administrative closure action is linked to the original BIS permit? This request is not for a single-property lookup. It is a public-interest dataset request intended to help licensed electricians, electrical contractors, property owners, expeditors, design professionals, and DOB staff track legacy BIS electrical permits affected by the transition from BIS to DOB NOW. The requested dataset should include, where available: - BIS job/control number - BIS permit number - Borough - BIN - Block and lot - Property address - Licensee name - Business name - Electrical license number - Permittee - BIS permit/application status - Abandoned status - Inactive status - Location Problem status - Objection flag - Objection status - Original filing date - Permit issue date - Permit expiration date - Abandonment/status date - Last BIS update date - DOB NOW job number, if linked - DOB NOW filing number, if linked - DOB NOW reinstatement flag - Referenced BIS job/control number entered in DOB NOW - DOB NOW filing status - DOB NOW permit status - DOB NOW inspection status - Pass-Final date - Complete date - BIS inactive date - Administrative closure date - Closure reason - Work type - Electrical scope summary - Job description The most important data element requested is the link between an abandoned BIS electrical permit and any DOB NOW: Build filing that reinstates, refiles, satisfies, or administratively closes that BIS permit. DOB guidance indicates that abandoned BIS electrical permits may be reinstated in DOB NOW: Build, but there does not appear to be a clear public dataset/API that allows the public to track this transition from BIS to DOB NOW. Publishing this dataset would improve transparency, reduce duplicate filings, support compliance tracking, help licensed electricians and owners resolve old permits, and provide a clearer public record of how legacy BIS abandoned electrical permits are being handled after the DOB NOW transition.
requests.response: Hello, we received your inquiry from the NYC Open Data Helpdesk. Our response is as follows: We are in the process of reviewing which field attributes you have mentioned below may be added to an existing DOB NOW data view in a future release. -- Department of Buildings (DOB)

requests.request: NYC's 2019 Open Data plan listed a Department of Finance dataset titled “Coop Data File 2018/19,” with a planned publication date of January 31, 2020. It is not identifiable in the current catalog under that title. Please determine whether it was published, renamed, superseded, deferred, or withdrawn. If it exists, please provide its stable dataset ID and URL. If it was not published, please identify the current status, responsible agency, and conclusive reason it is unavailable. Please also evaluate publication of the planned FY2018/19 file and a privacy-minimized current successor containing: borough-block-lot; cooperative/development identifier; apartment/unit identifier; residential/commercial or other unit type/status; unit shares; total cooperative shares; percentage of total shares if maintained; applicable/effective year or date; active/inactive/combined/split/superseded status; and non-personal stable identifiers needed to join releases. Please include a data dictionary, record layout, code tables, release cadence, data-as-of/effective dates, fiscal-year coverage, status/supersession rules, stable dataset and record IDs, needed RPAD/successor-system crosswalks, source/provenance, and known completeness limitations. Exclude shareholder/owner names, mailing addresses, SSN/TIN, primary-residence indicators, exemption/abatement eligibility, financial-account information, and confidential tax-return/supporting-document information. This would allow reproducible research and validation of NYC cooperative property assessment estimates without publishing personal information. Please confirm whether these non-personal records qualify as a public dataset under the NYC Open Data Law and, if so, provide an expected publication date or next administrative step. If not, please give the final reason and identify any public dataset that supersedes it.
requests.response: Based on the description, this data is available in another dataset. You should use the NYC Open Data Property Valuation and Assessment Data Tax Classes 1,2,3,4 dataset. (https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Property-Valuation-and-Assessment-Data-Tax-Classes/8y4t-faws/about_data) - For a list of condos, filter where - YEAR = 2027 - PERIOD = 3 (i.e., the final) - CONDO_NUMBER is not null - For a list of cooperative properties, filter where - YEAR = 2027 - PERIOD = 3 (i.e., the final) - COOP_NUM is not null

requests.agency: Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
requests.request: I am requesting that DOHMH publish Community Health Survey estimates aggregated at the Neighborhood Tabulation Area (NTA) geography rather than only at the larger United Hospital Fund neighborhood and community district geographies currently available. Core measures of interest include adult diabetes prevalence, adult obesity prevalence, adult hypertension prevalence, self-reported physical activity in the past 30 days, and self-rated health status. Multi-year estimates from 2018 forward would be ideal where sample sizes permit reliable NTA-level reporting. The question this data would help answer: how do chronic disease prevalence and physical activity patterns vary within community districts, not just across them? Current geographies are too coarse to surface meaningful within-neighborhood disparities. Brownsville is one community district but contains multiple NTAs with substantially different health profiles. Aggregating at NTA geography would allow researchers, foundations, hospital community benefit offices, and city agencies to identify and address disparities that current geographies obscure. Harmonizing health data to NTA geography would make cross-domain equity research substantially easier and would complement the recently submitted nominations for DPR rec center attendance, DYCD program enrollment, DPR free public programs, and DFTA older adult center fitness participation data.
requests.response: The Community Health Survey is sampled at the UHF level to 1) be able to generate reliable estimates at the UHF level and 2) lessen the chance of respondent identification based on survey data. UHFs are an aggregation of zip codes (see here for more information: https://www.nyc.gov/assets/doh/downloads/pdf/ah/zipcodetable.pdf). Since the data are not sampled at the NTA or census track level, we cannot generate estimates for that geography.

requests.request: I'm using the PDF reports provided (https://www.nyc.gov/assets/rentfreeze/downloads/pdf/scrie/tenant_status_docket/scrie_tenant_report_12_mos_by_docket_brooklyn.pdf) about SCRIE applications + approvals, but wanted to ask about sharing documentation and getting access to this data through the Open Data Portal, rather than pulling from PDFs. Some initial questions I have that your documentation would probably help me understand: How do we interpret the various application types? What does it mean for a docket number to show up several times? Can we use this data to understand how long applications took to approve? There appear to be “benefits start” before “application approved” so I think there’s nuance in the process I don’t understand. Thank you!
requests.response: 1. Rent Freeze application types: - Initial Application – Submitted when a tenant applies for SCRIE/DRIE for the first time. - Renewal Application – Required every 1–2 years, depending on the tenant’s renewal cycle, to maintain program benefits. - Benefit Transfer Application – Used when a tenant moves to a new rent‑regulated apartment and needs to transfer their existing Rent Freeze benefit. - Benefit Takeover Application – Submitted when the current SCRIE/DRIE beneficiary is no longer the head of household, and an eligible household member seeks to assume the benefit. - Redetermination Application – A benefit review process used to reassess a household’s eligibility and frozen rent amount when there is a significant change or discrepancy, such as a substantial income change or updated household information. 2. Docket number definition: A docket number is the unique SCRIE/DRIE case identifier assigned by the NYC Department of Finance. Each docket represents a tenant’s Rent Freeze benefit record for the full duration of their participation in the program. Because each lease period or benefit adjustment is processed as a separate application under the same docket, the docket number will appear repeatedly in the report. 3. Application processing time: The data provided cannot be used to determine how long applications took to be approved. 4. Benefit start date vs. application approval date: In the Rent Freeze Program, the benefit start date may precede the application approval date. This occurs because tenants are permitted to apply retroactively, and DOF calculates benefit based on the effective date of eligibility rather than the date the application is approved/processed.

requests.request: I am requesting access to the ZIP Code Boundaries dataset (ID: i8iw-xf4u), which includes geographic boundaries for NYC ZIP codes and their associated boroughs or counties. Use Case: My goal is to determine—programmatically—whether a given address using a Queens neighborhood name (e.g., Astoria, NY or Jamaica, NY) falls within Queens County (NYC) or outside city limits (e.g., Nassau County). This is critical because NYC and surrounding jurisdictions apply different real estate transfer tax rates. Why This Dataset Matters: The ZIP Code Boundaries dataset would allow me to cross-reference ZIP codes with borough boundaries, enabling us to apply the correct municipal transfer tax rate for each property. Without this data, it's difficult to distinguish between similarly named areas in Queens and nearby counties. Core Data Elements Needed: - ZIP code boundaries - Borough or county identification per ZIP - Polygon geometry to assess jurisdiction by coordinates This information is vital for providing homeowners with accurate closing cost estimates and promoting transparency in NYC real estate transactions.
requests.response: ZIP code data is not currently maintained by any NYC agency and NYC Open Data does not generally publish information that the City's government does not maintain. As you may be aware, ZIP codes are assigned by the United States Postal Service and used to designate mail routes. Furthermore, they are stored by USPS as points, not polygons, so do not represent a specific geographic boundary. If you would like to view the boundaries of ZIP codes you can: - use the US Census's Zip Code Tabulation Areas (ZCTAs) (https://www.census.gov/programs-surveys/geography/guidance/geo-areas/zctas.html). This site also contains more context on ZIP codes, and how they should and should not be used. - use ESRI's ZIP code areas (https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=8d2012a2016e484dafaac0451f9aea24), sourced from TomTom In either case, please note that since ZIP codes represent federal mail routes they can sometimes cross county and state lines. In addition, you can programmatically check ZIP codes for NYC addresses using the Department of City Planning's geocoding tools, including their online tool (https://www.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=8d2012a2016e484dafaac0451f9aea24), desktop tool (https://www.nyc.gov/content/planning/pages/resources/geocoding/geosupport-desktop-edition), or API (https://geoservice.planning.nyc.gov/). Hope this is helpful, and please do let us know if you have further questions.

requests.request: I would like to have tree planting, tree death, and tree removal data (ideally for each tree, with geocode of trees provided). I noticed there are such data online after 2018, and would like to have the data before 2018 as well, if possible.
requests.response: Hi Chang, Our apologies for the delayed response! Please see below: The forestry datasets come from our in-house application for tree asset management called the Forestry Management System (ForMS). There are two factors impacting the issues that you are experiencing. 1. The current iteration of ForMS was launched in 2015 and was populated using data collected during the 2015 tree census. For trees planted before 2015, “Planted Date” data was not collected during the tree census and Parks’ limited legacy planting records (2008–2015) could not be linked to census data due to technical and capacity constraints. 2. Improved and more robust data management and quality standards were implemented in 2018 leading to more complete records afterwards. Therefore, in general, the Planted Date field is NULL for trees planted before 2015, only somewhat consistently used for newly planted trees post 2015, and only more consistently used after 2018 (although it is still not 100% consistently used due to human error). In general, to get the most complete data for tree planting and tree removals for 2017-present, we suggest: 1. Use the Forestry Work Orders dataset, and then join that data to the Forestry Inspections dataset via Inspection Global ID, and then join Inspections to Forestry Planting Spaces and Forestry Tree Points via their respective GlobalIDs. a. For tree plantings: To approximate Date Planted where it is missing from the Tree Point, use Work Order “Actual Finish Date” for Closed status Tree Planting Category Work Orders (these generally match or are close enough together get a good approximation). b. For tree removals: Use “Actual Finish Date” from the Forestry Work Orders dataset For data prior to 2015, a FOIL request will have to be submitted.

requests.request: I'd like the FMSID to be added as a column to this dataset. --> https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Capital-Projects-Dashboard-Citywide-Schedule-Histo/95tx-snak/about_data You can see that this data exists by looking at this city-produced app that uses FMSID to join the history table with the project table: https://app.powerbigov.us/view?r=eyJrIjoiMTkwYWMyNGEtMDNiZC00OTY4LTk4YjEtYzI0MzhlOTA3MzllIiwidCI6IjM1YzgyODE2LTZjNTYtNDQzYi1iYWY2LTgzMTIxNjNjYWRjMSJ9 Thank you!
requests.response: The Capital Projects Dashboard comprises four distinct datasets: 1. Citywide Budget and Schedule: Contains the comprehensive combination of schedules and budgets. 2. Citywide Budget and Spend by Fiscal Year: Provides a detailed breakdown of the current budget allocations and expenditures for each fiscal year. 3. Citywide Budget Spend History and Variance: Includes historical data on budget allocations and actual spending, alongside variance calculations for each budget line item. 4. Citywide Schedule History and Variance: Presents historical scheduling data, including variances, for each agency-managed project. Each dataset utilizes two distinct identifiers: - FMSID: A unique identifier corresponding to individual budget line items. - PID: Recently introduced, this identifier represents an agency-managed project with its associated schedule. Dataset #4 (Citywide Schedule History and Variance) pertains exclusively to schedule history and therefore does not include the FMSID. We are not planning to add FMSID to this dataset because FMSID refers to budget line items, not schedule, and therefore there may be several FMSIDs for each row of data. However, to associate budgets with specific schedules, Dataset #1 (Citywide Budget and Schedule) can be referenced, as it demonstrates the many-to-many relationships between agency-managed projects (PID) and budget line items (FMSID).

requests.response: The Department of City Planning (DCP) publishes NYC population data based on the Census Bureau data. They collect the decennial census counts and then release American Community Survey (ACS) estimates every year based on the survey. For annual population data: - You can download annual ACS data from US Census Bureau here. - Once ACS data is released, we release NYC ACS tables here - 2024 not available yet - 2023 at NTA, CDTA and City Council districts not available yet - for earlier versions see the Archive tab at the bottom of the page For different geography levels. The US Census Bureau collect data at various geography levels including Census Block and Census Tract. To accurately aggregate data to higher geography levels, those geographies must use census blocks or tracts as building block. DCP has created tabulation areas at the neighborhood and community district level for this reason. You can download the Neighborhood Tabulation Areas (NTA) or Community District Tabulation Areas (CDTA) boundaries here. - 2020 NTA (boundaries only) - 2020 CDTA (boundaries only) - 2020 Census Tracts to 2020 NTAs and CDTAs Equivalency Table Police Precincts is a geography that does not align to Census Tracts so that is not a dataset that is published. You can reach out to NYPD to see if they have something they produce and publish. You may also be interested in our Population Fact Finder (PFF) app that consolidates US Census and ACS data at many geography levels over many time periods.

requests.response: There are several options to obtain address and square footages with a list of BBLs. First, you could download PLUTO or MapPLUTO and join your csv to PLUTO. PLUTO is a tax lot based dataset with property, building, and other geographic information. You can join your csv to either PLUTO or MapPLUTO by joining the BBL field. You can then select the Address and Lot Area (LotArea) fields for the info you are looking for. For more information about the fields or attributes included in PLUTO please see the PLUTO Data Dictionary. 1. PLUTO is a CSV as well. If you do not have GIS software you can download this CSV and join them together (How to join tables in excel) 2. MapPLUTO is available as a shapefile or file geodatabase. If you have GIS software you can use either version. Note there is a shoreline clipped and water included version of the spatial files. Second, you could use one of our GeoCoder applications. Use BL function for BBLs to address look up. This will not have property square footage info. 1. Geoservice: Geoservice is NYC Department of City Planning’s web service interface to the core Geosupport system. It exposes all Geosupport functions through simple and easy to use REST representations. Please note: To ensure equitable sharing among all users, we have limited Geoservice to 10,000 records a user per 24 hours. Once this number is exceeded, the user will be blocked from accessing Geoservice for 24 hours. Users can request an access key by emailing *****@planning.nyc.gov 2. Geosupport Desktop Edition: Download the desktop geocoding application and consult the user guide or FAQ if you have any questions.

requests.response: Thank you for contacting the NYC Open Data Helpdesk. We have monthly backups of this file that we can share, but the spring 2022 backup is likely not be what you want. Some more background from ***, cc’ed, whose team manages this data. We rely heavily on orthoimages for drawing building footprints, but the date of the orthoimages doesn’t always align with the version of the archived building data. For us, orthos serve as a reference rather than the source for new building data. Here are a few key points to clarify: · The orthoimages were captured between March 16–30, 2022, but we didn’t receive the final version until late 2022 due to the extensive processing and QA required before release. · Once the new orthos were received, we began using them as a reference. However, we don’t typically analyze or research them for new buildings. Currently, we’re still using the 2022 orthos to create new building footprints. · The 2022 planimetric data was created using the 2022 orthos. We received the planimetric data in 2024 and compared this data with the building footprints and made some updates. To answer your question: The building archive dataset from spring 2022 does not include any input from the 2022 orthos because we did not receive the orthos until fall 2022. Please feel free to follow up with *** to clarify further and let me know if we can help with anything here.

requests.request: Request a new dataset containing ALL violation responses submitted on nyc.gov/disputeticket. The dataset must include all "valid" and "invalid" violation numbers, as submitted, as part of a response, without modification. Specifically, "valid" being the 10-digit violation number used by the NYC Department of Finance to track violations and "invalid" being the 10-digit violation number with a dash between the 9th and 10th digit, as it appears on The City of New York Notice of Parking Violation aka, parking ticket. The dataset must also include any information regarding modifications to any data as entered on the website, the disposition of the violation entered, and the date and time of any modification / disposition, made by the Department Of Finance to / on every response submitted by the end user via the nyc.gov/disputeticket website. Dataset need background: The City of New York Notice of Parking Violation aka "ticket" (placed on the windshield of vehicles alleged of a violation) has a 10 digit number with a dash between the 9th and 10th digit. The New York City Department of Finance parking violations system seems to use a 10-digit violation number without the dash. This discrepancy results in "Notices of Impending Default Judgment" being issued to vehicle owners, with penalties and interest for not responding to a violation (with the 10-digit number without the dash) even though the vehicle owner submitted a response using a dash in the 10-digit violation number. Furthermore, violation responses submitted on nyc.gov/disputeticket with a 10-digit violation number with a dash (or submitted within minutes of when a violation is issued by the Traffic Agency) seem to be deleted from the DOF system making it impossible to prove to a Traffic Court Judge that the vehicle owner's response to an alleged violation was made online in a timely fashion. The primary use of this new dataset will allow one to estimate the number of individuals that have not been able to adequately dispute a ticket and estimate how much revenue is generated in fines, penalties and interest because of the 10-digit violation number w/ or w/o a dash discrepancy.
requests.response: Response not sent yet.

requests.agency: Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD)
requests.request: I need a list of buildings in NYC with rental units, the number of units, and the owner information. I am doing a project to determine the building owners with the most units.
requests.response: Thank you for contacting the NYC Open Data Helpdesk and your inquiry. First, you can access the universe of all buildings in NYC by accessing the Department of City Planning (DCP)'s PLUTO dataset on NYC Open Data. This dataset will provide you with an identifier (BBL) you can merge with the data HPD has on owners as well as the count of the number of total units (UnitsTotal) and count of the number of residential units (UnitsRes). The PLUTO dataset has tax lot owner information (OwnerName), but we cannot speak to how that data point is populated. Then you combine the HPD Multiple Dwelling Registrations and Registration Contacts open datasets RegistrationID to connect the ownership and building information data. The Multiple Dwelling Registrations dataset has the Boro, Block, and Lot that you can combine to create the BBL that will connect these data to PLUTO. The Registration Contacts dataset has building ownership information. Please note that it is challenging to have a comprehensive list of owners, as properties are registered under different LLCs. requests.request: Hello, I want to create a Python program for a fun project where users can search for an address and get tax block and lot information. I tried using web scraping, but it wasn't successful. I was wondering if you have an API or a complete NYC property records file that I could use. It would help streamline the process of accessing property data and enhance user experience. Thank you for considering my request.
requests.response: We received your inquiry from the NYC Open Data Helpdesk. Our response is as follows: The best option for property data in PLUTO (tabular) or MapPLUTO (spatial), which can be downloaded from our website. MapPLUTO is also available as a REST service via ArcGIS online. They are both a comprehensive list of every tax parcel in NYC. NYC tax parcels are commonly referred to as BBLs – Borough / Block / Lot because BBLs consist of a 10-digit number made up by a one-digit borough code, five-digit block id, and four-digit lot id. PLUTO/MapPLUTO does contain a primary address field but is not always reliable. Please review the PLUTO data dictionary and readme file for questions on using those files. We would recommend using the Address Points file for address look ups. You may also be interested in the Property Address Directory (PAD) and the Street Name Dictionary (SND). We also have several geocoder applications that perform sophisticated functions similar to the python program you are interested in creating. - Geoservice: https://geoservice.planning.nyc.gov/ - Geosupport Desktop Edition (download): https://www.nyc.gov/site/planning/data-maps/open-data/dwn-gde-home.page - Geographic Online Address Translator (GOAT): https://a030-goat.nyc.gov/Goat/ Best, Department of City Planning (DCP)

requests.request: I'm looking for a listing of all residential and commercial buildings by community district. I need CD, BIN, Block, Lot, house number, street address, and zip code.
requests.response: There is not a comprehensive list of all residential and commercial buildings that we are aware of but there are several datasets or geocoding applications that you could query to return the results you are looking for. PLUTO or MapPLUTO: these two datasets are published by the Department of City Planning (DCP) and contains extensive land use and geographic data at the tax lot level for every tax lot in NYC. PLUTO is available in a tabular format (csv). MapPLUTO is available in a spatial format (shapefile or geodatabase). Make sure to consult the PLUTO Data Dictionary and Readme files for more information or if you have additional questions. - Pros: - This contains zoning and land use fields. - If you are looking for all lots zoned residential or commercial, you should filter this dataset on ZoneDist1 and ZoneDist2 fields for all values that begin with “R” or “C” - If you are looking for all lots that have a land use of residential or commercial, you should filter this dataset on LandUse field for all values 01 – 05 - This also contains fields for CD, BIN, Block, Lot (& full BBL – borough, block, lot), address and zip code (at the lot level) - Cons: - This is a tax lot level dataset – tax lots can contain multiple buildings. - Will not contain info for every building, only primary building. - Lots that contain campuses like NYCHA complexes, colleges, sub-divisions will only contain info for primary building If you need every building you could download the Building Footprint data published by the Office of Technology and Innovation (OTI). This is comprehensive of all buildings in NYC and contains BIN but does not contain any of the other attribute information you are looking for. There is a MapPLUTO BBL so you could join it back to MapPLUTO to filter for zoning/land use and to retrieve the other attributes. See metadata here. You may also be interested in Address Points – they were initially created from data in the DCP Property Address Directory (PAD) file. Points were created approximately five feet inside building footprints along the correct street frontage. A field collection/verification process was undertaken to validate "multi-valued" addresses contained in the PAD file (i.e. those locations with a range of addresses). Additionally, a statistical sample of PAD single valued addresses was field checked. Approximately 100,000 locations were visited (about 10% of the total). This contains BIN, address, and zip code, but none of the other attributes. You also must use another file to determine if they were Residential or Commercial properties. See metadata here. If you have GIS capabilities, you could spatially join or select building foot prints or address points to the DCP zoning district files to determine residential or commercial zoning. Lastly, DCP has several geocoding applications that allows you to enter input (addresses, BBLs, BINs, etc.) and return other geographic data associated with that property based on the search type (Function Type). 1. GeoService API: The Geoservice API is a RESTful web service interface to the NYC Department of City Planning’s core Geosupport system. Geosupport is a geocoding system used by NYC government. Geosupport provides coordinate and geographic attributes for supported input locations (address, intersection, blockface, BIN, BBL). Geoservice exposes all the Geosupport functions through simple and easy to use REST representations. Allows for batch runs (multiple records). 2. Geosupport Desktop Edition: is a highly customized geocoding package that allows users to process geographic information for New York City. Allows for batch runs (multiple records). 3. Geographic Online Address Translator (GOAT): allows you to enter a New York City geographic location (such as an address, intersection, street segment, street stretch, block and lot or BIN), and returns related geographic property and political information (such as cross streets, side of street, tax block and lot (AKA Parcel–ID), five-digit ZIP code, census tract and block, police precinct, community district and city council district). Single record search only, no batch runs. If you have any follow up questions, first consult the data dictionaries, readme, and metadata files. If you still have questions about DCP data, you can reach out to us via DCPopendata@planning.nyc.gov. Thank you, -DCP Open Data Team

requests.request: Average Living Cost and Household Income from years 2000 to year 2024 I want to know What is the trend of Average Living Cost and Household Income since the year 2000
requests.response: Census data is your best option and it can be accessed from data.census.gov. However, we at the Department of City Planning (DCP) provide several US Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data for NYC. For Household Income our Population division recommends using median household income as a comparable variable across time. The dollar value needs to be inflated to the latest year available (2022). - 2000: https://www.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/planning-level/nyc-population/census2000/sf3incp1.pdf - Census tract level data are also available on our site—will need to be converted to 2020 geogs: https://www.nyc.gov/site/planning/planning-level/nyc-population/socio-tables-2000.page - ACS data: https://www.nyc.gov/site/planning/planning-level/nyc-population/american-community-survey.page. (1-year data should be used for city and boros, and 5-year data for tracts, NTAs, etc.) Average living cost is not a variable from the Census or ACS, but you could use other variables like “gross rent as a percent of household income” or “selected monthly owner costs as a percentage of household income” as proxies, both of those are also available from the 2000 Census and ACS (housing profile). Thank you, -DCP Open Data Team

requests.request: I'm trying to understand the overall street area in sqft of Manhattan. Overall sqft of streets in Manhattan. Overall sqft of buildngs in Manhattan. We're working on an academic book and we'd like to know if data like this currently exists. We'd like to understand how much of Manhattan's real estate is street scape.
requests.response: This might be more nuanced then one would expect. There are different types of street categories in NYC including, mapped streets, paper streets, unmapped streets, private streets, etc. Mapped Streets are right-of-ways and cannot be built on, same as mapped parks. However, a paper street is a mapped street but does not exist as a physical street, it is only mapped on the official City Map. Unmapped streets are not of the official city map but do exist as physical streets in some cases they are classified as private streets. If you are looking to use mapped streets I would use the Digital City Map (DCM) dataset (specifically the DCM feature class or shapefile) created by us, the Department of City Planning (DCP). You could filter the data by feature type like mapped streets and/or others. Read through the metadata to see other feature types. You could convert them from lines to polygons and use that to clip from the Manhattan Borough Boundary and calculate overall square footage. If you want to use physical streets, note they maybe subterranean or on private property, you could use the Roadbed and Sidewalk datasets together to clip from Manhattan Borough Boundary and calculate overall square footage. Note: both roadbed and sidewalk datasets are derived from 2022 ortho-imagery (aerials) as part of the Planimetrics dataset produced by NYC Office of Technology and Innovation (OTI). For more info see the github page. For buildings use the buildings footprint dataset. You clip from the Manhattan Borough Boundary and calculate overall square footage. Thank you, -DCP Open Data Team

requests.request: Thank you for reviewing our request. We are looking for textual description of traffic intersections in New York city. We hope the description is rich and it can touch upon as many perspectives as possible. For instance, such a description can cover nearby facilities (e.g. hospitals, schools, etc.), landmarks (e.g., historic buildings, parks, etc.) important traffic hubs (e.g. bridges, subway stations, etc.), landscapes (e.g., up/down hill, narrow road, etc.) and many more. It's also OK for the data to be outdated, like the ones old traffic report, city planner report, etc. Overall, we hope the volume of the data to be large and the context to be rich. The reason for the request is explained in the next question. Thank you. We are a research team from Cornell University, Computer Science Department. We are creating a multi-modal machine learning model for a smart city traffic system. The idea is that we can train computer-visioned-based machine learning models to control the traffic light for a small set of traffic intersections. Then we can recommend the model to control traffic in a similar intersection. However, determining 2 traffic intersections are so similar that they can share the same traffic control model is a non-trivial task. We plan to train a multi-modal model to solve the model recommendation problem. We have already collected intersection image data from wikimedia commons. Per our knowledge, NYC opendata has tabular data for intersections to summarize the traffic condition. (If there are more similar data sources, please share your insight with us.) We still hope to have the textual data to describe the intersections so that we can make a more educated recommendation. Suggestions, like where to look for such datasets, are also greatly appreciated. Thank you in advance.
requests.response: Your requested dataset is not maintained by New York City Department of Transportation (NYC DOT), all intersections are tracked by the street names, descriptions such as landmarks, subway stations, landscapes are not used as they can change over time and these facilities are not maintained by NYC DOT. You may find all New York City intersections tracked by street names in the LION dataset: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/LION/2v4z-66xt/about_data Thank you, NYC Department of Transportation

requests.response: The Department of City Planning (DCP) creates two datasets, PLUTO™ which contains extensive land use and geographic data at the tax lot level in NYC, and MapPLUTO™, which is the spatial version of the data using tax lot features from the Department of Finance's (DOF) Digital Tax Map (DTM), both with and without Water Area (shoreline clipped). You can download the version you prefer on City Planning's open data website, BYTES of the BIG APPLE™. You should also refer to the PLUTO data dictionary and Read Me file for any questions related to the data. Thank you, -DCP Open Data Team -- There are two options that might work for connecting to PLUTO data as a service: - Open Data API for PLUTO. When on that page click on the Actions dropdown in upper right corner. Select the preferred variables and settings. - MapPLUTO Rest Service on ArcGIS Online. If you have additional questions please reach out to us at DCPopendata@planning.nyc.gov. It will be easier to communicate than through open data portal. Thank you, -DCP Open Data Team

requests.response: The ACRIS – Real Property Master dataset includes a field DOC. AMOUNT which holds the Total Consideration for Transfers and the Principal debt or obligation for Mortgages. For arm’s length transfers like the sale of a home between unrelated parties, the total consideration is the sales price and for most mortgages that are being used to buy a home, the principal debt or obligation is the mortgage amount subject to mortgage recording tax. As such the mortgage recording tax needed for your project can be computed from the principal debt or obligation. The ACRIS – Real Property datasets including the Master dataset with the DOC. AMOUNT field are available via the Open Data SODA API.

requests.response: Regarding the access points that feed the Walk-to-a-Park analysis you referenced, we do have a layer, however it's made specifically for this analysis and does not include all access points of a park. It only includes the ones at the edges of the park. For example, at large parks, where there are no through streets, mid-block entrances are omitted if there are entrances closer to the block's edge. This access point layer also includes sites that aren't under Parks jurisdiction (like schoolyards open to the public, state and federal parkland, and privately owned accessible spaces) because for purposes of "walking to a park" the jurisdiction is irrelevant. We also have another geospatial layer that was most recently updated in 2019 (although I do not have information on how complete the dataset was, even back then). If you are interested in either of these datasets, please let us know so that we can start the process of talking with our Legal division to share.

For information requests (documents, correspondence, etc.) we encourage you to submit a FOIL request via Open Records: https://a860-openrecords.nyc.gov/ FOIL stands for the Freedom of Information Law. The New York State Freedom of Information Law requires government agencies to provide records to the public upon request. The FOIL definition of records is very broad and includes information found in paper and electronic documents and audio and visual recordings. requests.request: I'm looking for a shapefile that delineates NYC's neighborhoods as defined by the city. I'm working on a project that involves collecting neighborhood shapefiles for cities across the United States.
requests.response: There are no official neighborhood boundaries in New York City. The Department of City Planning (DCP) created Neighborhood Tabulation Areas (NTAs) that are medium-sized statistical geographies for reporting Decennial Census and American Community Survey (ACS), created by aggregating 2020 census tracts. Although the NTA boundaries and their associated names roughly correspond with many neighborhoods commonly recognized by New Yorkers, NTAs are not intended to definitively represent neighborhoods, nor are they intended to be exhaustive of all possible names and understandings of neighborhoods throughout New York City. Additionally, non-residential areas including large parks, airports, cemeteries, and other special areas are represented separately within this dataset and are assigned codes according to their type (See NTAType field). Thank you, -DCP Open Data Team

requests.request: Publicly funded early care and education providers in New York City are required to screen all children in their program within 45 calendars days of enrollment. https://infohub.nyced.org/working-with-the-doe/early-childhood/early-childhood-educators/supporting-quality-care-and-instruction/screening-assessment. requests.response: The Department of City Planning (DCP) is not aware of an official, comprehensive list of all houses of worship in NYC. The closest data available is PLUTO or MapPLUTO, which are respectively, tabular and spatial datasets of all tax lots in NYC. requests.request: Among other things, The Department of Buildings (DOB) enforces LL196 which provisions that all NYC construction workers complete site safety training courses and have an identification card as proof of completion of their training. These cards are numbered "Training Connect Cards" (https://www.nyc.gov/site/buildings/safety/site-safety-training.page). Each card number is associated with a worker profile and this profile contains details of all training that was completed by the individual worker, and some additional data like expiration. The centralized database of all issued cards (Training Connect Card database) with card numbers, worker training profile (no PPI necessary), issue date, expiration date and issuers is managed and owned by the DOB. By law, construction actors/companies operating in the City need to verify the training records of the workers they employ via the Training Connect Card and determine if the card is genuine (fakes are known to circulate). Having access to the centralized Traning Connect Card database would allow these actors to verify the veracity of the records with a data query system. This will help hedge against safety risks, compliance risk, and create being alerted when a card is expiring or fake. Thank you.

requests.request: I am looking for daily traffic count data for multiple locations within NYC. The available dataset by NYDOT is the "Traffic Volume Counts" which includes segment ID but not geolocations (lat and long). Do you have the ones with lat/long (or matching between segment ids and lat/long of the center of the segment) We are working on an Air Quality project at Princeton University and we will use traffic data (among other features) to analyze, model, and predict the spatio-temporal changes of air quality within the city of New York.
requests.response: Thank you for your inquiry. The NYC Department of Transportation (NYC DOT) Traffic Volume Counts data is street block based and does not contain lat, long coordinates. The geographic data consists of street segment (city block) information rather than the location of the actual counter. The segmentID field is based on the LION data (linked below) from the NYC Department of City Planning (NYC DCP), mapping every street block and the bases for almost all City used geospatial data. Note: LION data is in geospatial shapefile format but possible to extract into CSV. The segmentID in Traffic Volume Counts data can be joined with LION to identify the City block where the count was taken place. LION data also contains XFrom, YFrom, XTo, YTo fields containing coordinates that may be closest to your request. The data is in X,Y and not Lat, Long, a Geographic Information System (GIS) application is need to convert the coordinates or to visualize the data. Datasets: NYC DCP LION:https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/LION... Geographic Information Systems (GIS) softwares to map X,Y coordinates: 1) QGIS- Free and Open Source 2) ArcGIS- ESRI software, license based Thank you, - NYC DOT Open Data Team
requests.answer: Pointed to data that already exists

requests.request: I am looking for trash collections routes and schedules. I am trying to map what streets have trash collection on what days
requests.response: DSNY does not have a publicly available dataset of specific truck routes but, we do publish on the DSNY Frequencies dataset on the OpenData portal. This dataset contains Citywide DSNY frequency boundaries for collection operations and provides the DSNY collection days for refuse and recycling for every DSNY section. Other relevant DSNY datasets on the OpenData portal include the following: - DSNY Zones - DSNY Districts - DSNY Sections NYC OpenData also publishes the NYC Street Centerline (CSCL) dataset which is a road-bed representation of New York City streets containing address ranges and other information such as traffic directions, road types, and segment types which you can use to connect collection day info to specific streets. If you have questions about the CSCL dataset, you would need to reach out to Office of Technology and Innovation. Another street dataset is the LION Single Line Street Base Map from NYC Planning which is also available on the OpenData portal: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/LION/2v4z-66xt/data?no_mobile=true. LION is a single line street base map representing the city's streets and other linear geographic features, along with feature names and address ranges for each addressable street segment. If you have questions about LION, you would need to reach out to City Planning. We hope you find this information helpful. Thank you, - NYC DSNY Open Data

You’d want to weight the participation scores with the “weights” field when calculating the mean score grouped by the NTA.18 field. You can find more in-depth information about it’s construction in our 2019-2020 VAR here: https://www.nyccfb.info/media/reports/voter-analysis-report-2019-2020/ Next week I’ll be giving a talk on the construction of the participation score, alongside the community organization Hester Street who will explain how they use the participation score for voter outreach, as part of NYC’s Open Data Week. It’s a free online event and you can RSVP here: https://2022.open-data.nyc/event/using-open-election-participation-data-to-inform-voter-outreach-in-nyc/#rsvp-now. requests.request: In 2014, New York City introduced the New York City enhanced real property tax credit, a refundable credit to qualifying renters residing in New York City. Between 2014 and 2019, renters could file tax form NYC-208 to claim the credit on their income taxes. My research partners and I want to use data from these filings to calculate rental prices at the property level. We are requesting the following variables from Form NYC-2018, for years 2014 through 2019: 1) address address, city/village/post office, state and ZIP code associated with the tax credit filing; Line 14: Household gross income; Line 17: Gross rent paid; Line 18: Adjusted rent (in case line 17 includes utilities). DOF makes the Condo-Rent equivalence data available with addresses, so we hope to get address-level data too. Average rent by address would also work. Housing court is where eviction cases are decided, and prior research suggests that there are economically meaningful pecuniary and non-pecuniary costs of being evicted for tenant households (Collinson et al., 2021). In response to this research, policy makers have introduced new programs to help tenants avoid eviction. Subsidized legal aid is a prominent example of such a program. In 2017, the City of New York was the first to promise accessible legal services to all tenants with income below a given income threshold and facing eviction proceedings (Office of Civil Justice, 2018). Proponents of this program argue that it helps prevent the costs to tenants of experiencing an eviction. Detractors argue that by making it more costly to evict a tenant, the program increases the effective cost of renting to low-income tenants, and that this cost may be passed on to tenants in the form of higher rent prices, higher deposits, decreased supply of rental housing units, or a lower likelihood of approval for rental applications from the lowest-income tenants. Recent research evaluates the effect of legal aid on the outcomes of eviction court cases (Gould Ellen et al., 2020). To gain a more complete picture of the effects of the policy, we will aim to evaluate the effect it has had on rent prices, rental housing supply, deposits, and landlords’ screening decisions.
requests.response: The data filed on the NYC-208 is considered private and is not available on Open Data. You may be able to obtain this data by requesting it through FOIL. Thank you, - NYC DOF

requests.agency: Department of Youth and Community Development (DYCD)
requests.request: We are requesting additional data not available in the publicly available dataset, DYCD Program Sites. a) Enrollment and budgeted capacity for afterschool programs during the school year and over the summer with data for: • COMPASS: COMPASS Elementary, COMPASS Explore, COMPASS High School, COMPASS Middle School, and COMPASS SONYC Pilot programs. • Beacons and Cornerstones b) Enrollment and budgeted capacity for other program areas, including: • Jobs and Internships, such as programs under SYEP program area (Ladders for Leaders (LFL), Younger Youth (YY), Older Youth (OY), SYEP School-Based, etc.), program area Advance and Earn (Advance and Earn, YAIP), program area WIOA (Learn and Earn, Train and Earn) and Opportunity Youth Support. • Literacy and Immigrant Services, such as ESL Civics, Immigrant Families, NDA Immigrant Services, Adolescent Literacy, and Adult Literacy. Afterschool programming and jobs/internships opportunities for children and youth during school year as well as summer opportunities, are important community resources that contribute to the well-being of children and youth they serve and their families. While DYCD already releases program location information, enrollment and capacity data provide more accurate information about the availability of these programs across New York City neighborhoods which vary in population density overall, and the demographic groups (e.g., children, youth, adults with limited English proficiency) most likely to utilize these programs. Site-level data with this additional information will allow us to provide more complete picture of afterschool and other youth services landscape in the city. Citizens’ Committee for Children of New York uses information on afterschool and other youth services as part of our ongoing analysis of public data on community-level conditions and trends, of which opportunities for youth are a key component. These data will be used as part of data resources, including Keeping Track Online (data.cccnewyork.org) and other publications. On Keeping Track Online, we present data on child and family well-being aggregated by Community Districts, Zip Codes, School District, as well as map of community resources. There resources include banks, child care, libraries, and afterschool programming locations from the DYCD Program Sites dataset, among others. We also use these data in reports, such as our community based assessment for Elmhurst-Corona, Queens: Community Driven Solutions to Improve Child and Family Well-being. In this publication, we used data on afterschool programming and youth services to illustrate opportunities for youth in specific community. In another publication, Keeping Track Of New York City’s Children: 2020, we report city-level trends on number of school-year and summer slots in afterschool programs (see page 34). These data resources offer multiple audiences who may rely on information on the needs and opportunities of children and families but do not have data analysis capacity on staff, including organizations that work with school-age children and provide education programming.

requests.request: I'm looking for a data set of all M zoned lots and corresponding lot sizes in NYC Trying to understand the amount acres in M (manufacturing) districts currently in each borough.
requests.response: The Department of City Planning (DCP) produces a dataset called MapPLUTO. PLUTO is a data file of NYC tax lots containing over seventy data fields derived from several NYC city agencies related to tax lot and building characteristics, geographic, political, administrative districts, and zoning. Before using the data it is recommended to consult both the ReadMe file and Data Dictionary. Determining Zoning: You can search MapPLUTO for zoning and lot size. The lots zoning can be found in ZoneDist1, ZoneDist2, ZoneDist3 and ZoneDist4. If multiple zoning districts are on a lot, the four largest are listed in ZoneDist1-4 fields, these are commonly referred to as split lots. You can search for lots that contain zoning districts that start with "M" to determine all the M-zoned lots. A few items to consider, if a lot has ZoneDist1 = R and ZoneDist2 = M, your search will identify this lot as M-zoned but only a portion of that lot is actually zoned for manufacturing. Also, there are mixed use zoning districts that allow for both residential and light manufacturing (e.g. M1-1/R5, M1-1/R7-2, etc.), these can be considered m-zoned but just note the actual use could be residential. These two examples are separate, the former is partially m-zoned and the latter is considered completely m-zoned. Determining Size: MapPLUTO has two fields related to lot size. LotArea: Total area of the tax lot, expressed in square feet rounded to the nearest integer. If the tax lot is not an irregularly shaped lot (see IRREGULAR LOT CODE) the Department of Finance (DOF) culates the LOT AREA by multiplying the LOT FRONTAGE by the LOT DEPTH. If the tax lot is irregularly shaped, DOF calculates the LOT AREA from the Digital Tax Map. Note: this field can be null or blank. If this is blank use ShapeArea ShapeArea: Total area of the tax lot,expressed in square feet, as the GIS geometry is drawn and not based on official tax lot dimensions from DOF. Alternative Analysis: If you have GIS skills/knowledge, you could use DCP's zoning district file from our NYC GIS Zoning Features dataset - download the shapefile package. Select only M-districts in the zoning district file, then use that selection to clip MapPLUTO. The area left would be the portions of lots only M-zoned and you could use the shape area to determine the total M-zoned area. Please refer to the readme and data dictionary for further questions.
requests.answer: Pointed to data that already exists

requests.request: The number of homeless individuals located in City Council District 30, Community Board 5 and the borough of Queens, broken down by zip code. Geographical data on homeless individuals housed at the Cooper Rapid Rehousing Center. Provide data on which zip codes and community board districts residents lived in prior to moving into a shelter. We are attempting to address the homelessness crisis in New York City.
requests.response: Thank you for your dataset requests. With regards to the request for the number of homeless individuals by City Council District, Community Board, and ZIP Code: The Agency currently publishes on Open Data for the number of homeless individuals by Borough and Community District and that is here: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Social-Services/Individual-Census-by-Borough-Community-District-an/veav-vj3r. For the other breakdowns requested, while this data is theoretically present in Agency data systems in the form of individual disaggregated records, the Agency does not maintain an existing report split by City Council District or ZIP code. Please note, because the data requested is not maintained in the format requested, production of the data for this specific, single request would require significant new programming involving significant Agency resources and therefore cannot be provided with reasonable effort. See Public Officers Law, Article 6, Sec. 89(3)(a). Additionally, pursuant to Public Officer Law (POL) § 87(2)(a), release of such information is prohibited by NY Social Services Law § 136 since production could reveal personally identifiable information, including but not limited to the location of the various shelter sites. Even if data were able to be reasonably produced and provided in a seemingly aggregated form without undue burden, which it is not, that data could still be utilized to identify confidential shelter locations, since the specificity of the information, such as ZIP code, for example, which reflects a very small geographical area/tract, could be cross-examined and triangulated with existing public information to reveal the locations of confidential shelter facilities and the locations where public benefits recipients are residing, in violation of NY SSL § 136, as indicated. Additionally, such a release could also constitute an unwarranted invasion of privacy and violation of client confidentiality pursuant to POL § 87(2)(b). With regards to the request for specific data about specific clients who are currently experiencing homelessness and residing at a specific confidential/protected shelter location, in this case for their prior home addresses before they lost their housing and entered shelter: While this data is present in Agency data systems in individual disaggregated records, the Agency does not maintain an existing aggregated report with the addresses of individuals prior to entering DHS for specific shelters nor can such a report be provided with reasonable effort. See Public Officers Law, Article 6, Sec. 89(3)(a). Moreover, pursuant to Public Officer Law (POL) § 87(2)(a), release of such information is a violation of client confidentiality protections, prohibited by NY Social Services Law § 136, since production would reveal confidential case information such as prior residences/addresses for public benefits recipients and/or personally identifiable information by revealing client identities. Additionally, such a release could also constitute an unwarranted invasion of privacy and violation of client confidentiality pursuant to POL § 87(2)(b). Please email me at drinkwatere@dss.nyc.gov for any further questions on this topic. Sincerely, Erin Drinkwater Deputy Commissioner, Intergovernmental & Legislative Affairs NYC Department of Social Services

The TLC used to provide a hashed driver/vehicle identifier in taxi trip records to allow for driver and vehicle level analysis. Privacy advocates were able to re-identify these records and determine incomes and addresses of drivers and vehicle owners, so those fields have since been redacted in all datasets maintained by TLC or NYC Open Data. Copies of the data that contain the removed hashed identifiers exist but are not supported by TLC or the City of New York, and we make no claims to their accuracy. City agencies in NYC have the discretion to determine what qualifies as personally identifying information under the Freedom of Information Law, so FOIL requests asking for vehicle identifiers are dismissed under the PII exemption.

The DEP permitting process is on an equipment basis and the NYS DEC Title V permitting process is based on facility wide emissions. Title V source permits can be obtained in the NYS DEC website. https://www.dec.ny.gov/dardata/boss/afs/issued_atv.html Each Title V permit includes specific permit conditions including any emission monitoring requirements. DEP does not monitor for PM10 and NOx at major sources but NYS DEC has an air monitoring program. Thank you, - NYC Open Data Team

requests.request: Hello, this is a follow up to a previously requested a data layer the Flood Hazard Mapper web application named 'Base Flood Elevation (2015 PFIRMs)', with the attribute 'Elevation Above Grade" (it is the fourth item listed in the layer list). I believe the layer I need https://dcp.maps.arcgis.com/home/item.html?id=5268a74fd4b04a7894c9b85ef7a8a6a3 may have been developed by DCP by overlaying the FEMA BFE with the City's DEM. Can you please advise is you can send me this layer as a shapefile or geodatabase. Please call me at 949 235 6517 if it would help to discuss. Thank you. Potential flood vulnerability to electric utility facilities
requests.response: I cleared with our agency that we can share the data with you. Please submit an email to dcpopendata@planning.nyc.gov. The Open Data feedback platform does not allow us to see your email address. Once you send the request for the data I can make the data available through one of our data sharing platforms. I do want to point out that there are some limitations with this data including; This dataset is being provided by the Department of City Planning (DCP) for informational purposes only. DCP does not warranty the completeness, accuracy, content, or fitness for any particular purpose or use of the dataset, nor are any such warranties to be implied or inferred with respect to the dataset as furnished on the website. DCP and the City are not liable for any deficiencies in the completeness, accuracy, content, or fitness for any particular purpose or use the dataset, or applications utilizing the dataset, provided by any third party. Also, here is more detail about how the dataset was created and its purpose: FEMA’s Preliminary Flood Insurance Rate Maps (PFIRMs), released in 2015 as part of a citywide flood map update, are the best available flood hazard data for building code and planning purposes. They show areas vulnerable to flooding from 1% annual chance storm, also sometimes called the Special Flood Hazard Area or 100-year floodplain. They also show today’s 0.2% annual chance floodplain, also known as the 500-year floodplain. In addition to showing the extent of flooding, the PFIRMs also show Base Flood Elevations (BFE). BFEs are the computed elevation to which floodwater is anticipated to rise during a 1% annual chance storm, measured relative to the North American Vertical Datum of 1988 (NAVD88). Combining the height of the BFE above the ground elevation at the building’s location with required freeboard will determine the elevation to which a structure must be elevated or floodproofed to meet code requirements for new construction or to receive reduced flood insurance premiums. This layer displays the height of the 2015 PFIRM BFEs above ground elevation based on the 2010 NYC Digital Elevation Model. Property owners should consult a certified engineer or surveyor to determine the exact elevation of their structure in relation to the BFE. Thank you, - NYC DCP Open Data Team

If it is easier to speak by phone, please let me know the best time and number to call. Crime and Criminal Justice Response to the Coronavirus and Lockdowns: The global pandemic caused by the novel coronavirus and responses to it beginning in early 2020 has had far ranging impact. One domain where the effects are likely to be complex is crime and criminal justice. This paper has two aims: First, to aggregate data from major U.S. cities in order to get rapid and broad measures of the impact of the pandemic on crime. Second, to construct a simple model of crime in a pandemic and calibrate it using the aggregated data. The hope is that this effort may have both short and long-term utility, both in considering pandemic response and in our understanding of supply and demand for crime. Data From top 25 US cities: Time series of crime incidents and arrests from 2015 to present. (almost universally available) Shootings (available in some cities) Domestic violence incidents (available in some cities) Prison release data Individual movement data (e.g. from Google, Apple, SafeGraph) Covid prevalence data, including: positive diagnoses, total tests, deaths Critical dates including: Stay-at-home orders, social distancing orders, orders regarding policing, orders regarding prison releases, orders regarding detention policies for new arrestees, re-opening orders Key Questions How has crime incidence been impacted by a) the pandemic and b) lockdowns? How does this vary by crime type/region/offender characteristics? Same as above for arrests. Is crime data reliable? Can we use some crime types (like shootings and homicides) to tell whether incidence data may be under-reported? Can we identify an impact of different orders on crime? Can we use the abrupt pandemic-induced changes to estimate a simple model of crime?

The data you've downloaded is in NY State Plane Feet (Zone LI), also known as EPSG:2263. For a variety of reasons, DoITT will continue to maintain this data in this format. The data will only be used for Academic research purposes and here are some of the details that would be helpful in have in the dataset: • Type of Crime as assigned by the LA PD • Date of the reported crime • Textual narrative of the crime event ( as reported by the police officer) • Crime Code assigned • Crime Category ( as assigned by the LAPD) Additional Considerations: 1. Any other fields in addition to the above would definitely be useful but not necessary. Formal crime types are not discrete in topic space. Rather, crime types are distributed across a range of crime topics. Similarly, individual crime topics are distributed across a range of formal crime types. Key ecological groups include identity theft, shoplifting, burglary and theft, car crimes and vandalism, criminal threats and confidence crimes, and violent crimes. Though not a replacement for formal legal crime classifications, crime topics provide a unique window into the heterogeneous causal processes underlying crime. Keywords: Machine learning, Non-negative matrix factorization, Text mining, Crime I do not need any identifying information and therefore all and any identifying information can be removed prior to sharing the data. Kindly let me know if this is the right venue and method to request for such data and if anything else needs to be done in order to obtain this data. My analysis will help create new crime categories which would include the behavioral and situational aspect of the crime event as opposed to the current formal crime categories. requests.request: My name is *** and I am a candidate reseach for the *** looking for population data for the year 2012 for New York City. I am particularly interested in gridded population data. These can be in the .tiff format or shapefile format if available. If population data for the year 2012 is not avaialble. Previous year 2010 is also ok. I want to use these data as validation data at the pixel level. Using remote sensing datasets and population data at the county level, I want to produce population distribution maps. The provded grid, will be used as reference data.
requests.response: Population density might not be that accurate at a pixel level (depends on the size of your pixel). Census Blocks are the smallest unit that Census data is released - you need to download that from the US Census Bureau You can also explore more NYC US Census and American Community Survey (ACS) data on our New York City Population FactFinder app Additionally: The Department of City Planning (DCP) releases aggregated 5 year population estimates for NYC at the Neighborhood Tabulation Area (NTA) level based on American Community Survey (ACS) estimates. NTAs were created to project populations at a small area level, from 2000 to 2030 for PlaNYC, the long-term sustainability plan for New York City, using whole census tracts from the 2010 Census as building blocks. For population estimates at scales lower than the NTA you would have to obtain them from the US Census Bureau, but the reliability of those estimates may not be reliable (see ACS note below). ACS demographic profiles for NTA are available here: https://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/planning-level/nyc-population/american-community-survey.page -change the drop down year to 2014 (When looking for five-year ACS equivalents to one-year period, we advise to match the mid-year of the five-year estimate 5 year estimate (2010-2014) NTA boundaries are available here: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Neighborhood-Tabulation-Areas/cpf4-rkhq Notes about using ACS data: The ACS data is the most extensive nationwide survey currently available. From its annual releases, DCP is able to examine the city’s detailed demographic, social, economic, and housing characteristics. Each month, ACS questionnaires are sent to a sample of approximately 300,000 addresses across the country, so households are continuously receiving and responding to the ACS. In order to have a large enough sample from which to create estimates of characteristics for small areas, the ACS “rolls-up” the sample for five-year periods. New York City Population FactFinder (PFF) relies on these five-year period estimates to produce all of its ACS profile content. Because these estimates span a five-year period, they are represented with a start-year and end-year (for example, 2013-2017). These do not represent change over that five-year period, but rather something akin to a five-year average. It is also important to note that ACS estimates are derived from a survey and are subject to sampling error. Consequently, all ACS estimates are published with Margins of Error (MOEs) at a 90% confidence interval. These MOEs are available in PFF in data reliability views. ACS data in PFF are available at census tract-, Neighborhood Tabulation Area-, and Public Use Microdata Area-levels. Thank you, - DCP Open Data Team

requests.request: Good morning. As part of my PhD reseach project I am looking fo population data of the city of New York for the year 2012 and well as bulding footprint for the year 2012. I was able to obtain the Population Estimates at the County level and was wondering in population estimates are also available at the track or block level. I am working with population disaggregation methodologies and the data will be used fo validation. This data will not be shared or publisehd in any way. Additionally, I have been able to download the historic building footprint layer of New York, how ever there are properties on the table that are not clear for me, for example the "Demolition" and "Demolation Date", it is not clear for me, how can I "clean" the table to only obtain 2012 building footprints. I was wondering if this infomation can be provided. I am doing validation of settlement layers derived from remote sensing data. Population distribution maps are being produced on base of high resolution imagery and the data is needed for validation.
requests.response: The Department of City Planning (DCP) releases aggregated 5 year population estimates for NYC at the Neighborhood Tabulation Area (NTA) level based on American Community Survey (ACS) estimates. NTAs were created to project populations at a small area level, from 2000 to 2030 for PlaNYC, the long-term sustainability plan for New York City, using whole census tracts from the 2010 Census as building blocks. For population estimates at scales lower than the NTA you would have to obtain them from the US Census Bureau, but the reliability of those estimates may not be reliable (see ACS note below). ACS demographic profiles for NTA are available here: https://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/planning-level/nyc-population/american-community-survey.page -change the drop down year to 2014 (When looking for five-year ACS equivalents to one-year period, we advise to match the mid-year of the five-year estimate 5 year estimate (2010-2014) NTA boundaries are available here: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Neighborhood-Tabulation-Areas/cpf4-rkhq You can also explore more NYC US Census and ACS data on our New York City Population FactFinder app Notes about using ACS data: The ACS data is the most extensive nationwide survey currently available. From its annual releases, DCP is able to examine the city’s detailed demographic, social, economic, and housing characteristics. Each month, ACS questionnaires are sent to a sample of approximately 300,000 addresses across the country, so households are continuously receiving and responding to the ACS. In order to have a large enough sample from which to create estimates of characteristics for small areas, the ACS “rolls-up” the sample for five-year periods. New York City Population FactFinder (PFF) relies on these five-year period estimates to produce all of its ACS profile content. Because these estimates span a five-year period, they are represented with a start-year and end-year (for example, 2013-2017). These do not represent change over that five-year period, but rather something akin to a five-year average. It is also important to note that ACS estimates are derived from a survey and are subject to sampling error. Consequently, all ACS estimates are published with Margins of Error (MOEs) at a 90% confidence interval. These MOEs are available in PFF in data reliability views. ACS data in PFF are available at census tract-, Neighborhood Tabulation Area-, and Public Use Microdata Area-levels. The building foortprint data is released by DOITT so they would need to address your questions related to that dataset. Thank you, - DCP Open Data Team

requests.request: I'm looking for loans recorded on rent stabilized properties from 2012 through 2017 I'd like to understand how the new rent regulation laws affect these loans
requests.response: DOF is not the keeper of records for rent stabilized properties, but if you can obtain a listing, our ACRIS data will be able to provide information on loans recorded against the properties for the four boroughs of Manhattan, Bronx, Brooklyn, and Queens. Once a list of BBLs (Borough/Block/Lot) for rent stabilized properties is determined, this list can be matched with the ACRIS data in Open Data. To do so you will first need to download the ACRIS Real Property Master and ACRIS Real Property Legals dataset from Open Data. The ACRIS Real Property Legals dataset can then be filtered by the rent stabilized BBL list to determine the recordings for rent stabilized properties. These records can then be linked to the ACRIS Real Property Master dataset by DOCUMENT ID and GOOD_THROUGH_DATE fields. Finally the linked result can be further filtered by the using the RECORDED/FILED date to restrict to 2012 through 2017 and the DOC_TYPE field to limit to just loans. Most loans are MORTGAGEs and will appear under the DOC_TYPE code MTGE; however you may also be interested in other types of loans such as SMTG (the code for SUNDRY MORTGAGE), AL&R (the code for ASSIGNMENT OF LEASES AND RENTS) and occasionally AGMT (the code for AGREEMENT). See the ACRIS Document Control Codes dataset for a full list of document types than can be recorded in ACRIS. The ACRIS Real Property Master dataset can also provide basic details regarding the loan including the date of the loan (the DOC_DATE field) and the loan amount (the DOC_AMOUNT field) and the ACRIS Real Property Legals dataset can provide additional property details like property type (the PROPERTY_TYPE field) – see the ACRIS Property Type Codes dataset for a full list of property type codes and their descriptive meaning. Thank you, - NYC Open Data Team
