requests.request: We are looking for a list of residential buildings, square foot, amenities, units, developers, and property management in NYC. What residential buildings exist and its total square footage. How many buildings in NYC are operated by property management services, and by which property management company.
requests.response: Hi , You can get some of what you're looking for from Department of Buildings data. List of residential buildings Our DOB Job Application Filings dataset is a list of all of the active applications for construction work since 2000. This will give you a list of buildings throughout the city for those buildings that are subject to DOB oversight and that have done construction work in that time period. Older buildings that have not done any alterations since 2000 will not appear on this list. A small number of buildings that are not subject to DOB oversight, like some federal buildings, will not appear on this list. In the Building Class column, you will find a code that you can match to Department of Finance Building Class to find out if the building is residential. Developers For developer, you can get information about the Applicant, who must be a licensed design professional. This does not tell you what company they work for. Square footage In that same dataset if you scroll all the way to the right, you will find Total Construction Floor Area. This is only available for certain types of construction work where this number is required to be filled out. Dwelling units Similar to square footage, this is not required to be filled out for all types of construction work. For those that contain this information, you'll find Existing Dwelling Units, which is the number before construction, and Proposed Dwelling Units, which is the number after construction is complete. The other information you requested is not available at the Department of Buildings. Thank you, - DOB Open Data Coordinator

requests.response: Hi , Department of City Planning (DCP) puts out a dataset called PLUTO (table) or MapPLUTO (shapefile). This dataset contains every tax lot in the city, and contains attribute data on land use, building code, owner name and other property info. requests.request: I would like to know if it is possible to obtain historical records of active taxi medallions. My research group is trying to see how many taxi drivers start driving and how many drivers stop driving and how these entry and exit of drivers is related to the business cycle.
requests.response: Hi , Thanks for reaching out. Based on your requested dataset and the question you are trying to answer, I believe you are asking for two different things-- inactive medallions and inactive drivers. The taxi medallion is a permit which allows a vehicle to operate as taxi and accept street hails in the five boroughs, whereas the TLC driver's license allows a person to drive a taxi or for-hire vehicle (i.e. app car like Uber or Lyft, or traditional black car/livery/luxury limo service) in the five boroughs. The medallion vehicle may or may not be owned by the person who drives it as some taxis are part of fleets and most are leased, so an inactive medallion does not necessarily mean a driver has exited the market. Regardless, we already have an inactive medallion list on Open Data here: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Transportation/Medallion-Vehicles-Inactive/jgtb-hmpg With regard to inactive drivers, we only release the active driver lists on Open Data, though drivers who have been suspended or revoked could potentially be obtained with a FOIL request. However, it is worth noting that TLC's driver license is a universal license, meaning that the same license can be used to drive a taxi OR for-hire vehicle, so you would not be able to definitively say that a taxi driver has exited the market, only that a TLC-licensed driver has. If you would still like to make a FOIL request or inquire about the process, follow the instructions on this page: https://www1.nyc.gov/site/tlc/about/request-data.page Thank You, Taxi and Limousine Commission (TLC)

requests.response: Hi , The information you are looking for is not maintained by NYC Open Data as it is a request for multiple records likely from multiple systems for a specific location. To obtain this type of information (actual permits, work history documents, and possibly other), you will need to submit a FOIL request using Open Records: https://a860-openrecords.nyc.gov/ FOIL stands for the Freedom of Information Law. The New York State Freedom of Information Law requires government agencies to provide records to the public upon request. Government records affect the lives of each New Yorker, and providing easy access to the records makes government work better. The FOIL definition of records is very broad and includes information found in paper and electronic documents and audio and visual recordings. All records are available upon request, unless an exception in FOIL permits an agency to deny access to a record. Learn more about FOIL requests via this Frequently Asked Questions page. Thank you, - NYC Open Data Team

requests.request: How many hotel permits were granted each year from 2000 to now. How many new hotel rooms were permitted to be built each year. How many square feet of hotel rooms were permitted to be built each year from 2000 to now. How many new hotels were permitted to be built each year from 2000 to now. Thank you very much!
requests.response: Department of Buildings does not track construction specifically for hotels. You can find an approximation of what you're looking for in our data as follows: A construction job can have many different permits for everything from plumbing to a sidewalk shed. For your analysis, I suggest you look at the overall job application rather than individual permits so that you are not inflating your count. Use our DOB Job Application Filings dataset, which goes back to 1/1/2000. If you are looking for brand new buildings, you will want to filter Job Type for NB. In the Existing Occupancy and Proposed Occupancy columns, you'll see the occupancy classification. (Note: These fields are not required for every job.) You're looking for jobs that say "Res". This will indicate hotels and apartments, but it's a broad category that can mean other things too. (See page 19 of our PW1 User Guide for more detail.) We do not track hotel rooms, but we do track "dwelling units". You can find the numbers in the Existing Dwelling Units and Proposed Dwelling Units columns. (Note: These fields are not required for every job.) For square footage, your best bet is TOTAL_CONSTRUCTION_FLOOR_AREA. This does not differentiate between rooms and common areas, and like the other fields mentioned, this is not required for every job. Please check our Data Dictionary for additional information. (On the dataset information page, there's a link to it under Attachments.) Thank you, - DOB Open Data Coordinator

requests.agency: Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD)
requests.request: Historical data on multiple dwelling registrations, ideally starting from 2005. The effects of home ownership on children's outcomes. I would use this data to help better identify renter versus owner occupied buildings.
requests.response: Hi , Unfortunately, I do not think you can reliably identify homeowners vs renters using the Multiple Dwelling Registration data. It is not uncommon, for example, for a landlord owning a 4 unit (or larger) building to personally reside in that building while the other units are rental. That same landlord may register the building as owned by "Jane Smith" or owned by "123 Park St LLC" -- the registration information doesn't reveal homeowner/rental status. As you probably know, coop and condo buildings make up a large part of NYC's housing stock. It's very common for condo and coop buildings to contain renters in addition to homeowners. All of that said, the best proxy for this information that I’m aware of is through the NYC Dept. of Finance data. Citywide building data can be downloaded here: https://www1.nyc.gov/site/finance/taxes/property-assessments.page Building classification codes provide approximate data for rental vs. owned. There is no official guide on this, but what I can tell you is that, broadly speaking, building classes that start with “A” or “B” are small 1 or 2 family dwellings which may be owner occupied and/or rented. Building classes that start with “C” or “D” are rentals or co-ops, depending upon if the specific description for each contains the word co-op/cooperative. And classes that start with “R” are condo. https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/finance/jump/hlpbldgcode.html But again, buildings that with a co-op or condo building class may contain individual units that are being rented out at any given point in time - it's very common in my experience. I hope this is helpful. NYC Housing Preservation & Development (HPD)

requests.request: I'm looking for a dataset of all Public records relating to the transfer of ownership for residential buildings in the five boroughs. What is the frequency of turnover of privately held residential buildings in New York City.
requests.response: Hi , The ACRIS Real Property Master and Real Property Legals datasets would be a good starting point. To make better sense of the data, the ACRIS Document Control Codes and ACRIS Property Type Codes datasets would also be useful to identify which documents in the ACRIS Real Property Master dataset are transfers of ownership and which properties in the Real Property Legals dataset are residential building, respectively. DOF has other data which might be useful. For example sales files generated by the DOF Property division from ACRIS data would give another perspective on what ACRIS recordings are considered transfers of ownership. And as an additional example, the assessment roll files would help identify the building class for properties in the ACRIS Real Properties Legals dataset which would serve as a secondary way to identify residential building (with just the ACRIS datasets one would use the ACRIS property type). For Staten Island, ACRIS only has information about the NYC RPTT return and even then only going back to 2004. The underlying ownership changing documents for properties in Staten Island are recorded with the Richmond County clerk. Note that the Richmond County clerk is not a city official and as such is not bound by NYC Open Data laws so this information is not in NYC OpenData.

requests.request: DEPARTMENT OF FINANCE - ACRIS DATA: ALL COOPERATIVE APARTMENT SALES IN NYC, ADDRESS OF APARTMENT, NAME OF COOPERATIVE CORPORATION, NEW YORK CITY TRANSFER TAX AMOUNT, NEW YORK STATE TRANSFER TAX AMOUNT TRANSFER TAX AMOUNTS
requests.response: Hi , To find Cooperative Apartment Sales since 2003 (the only sales that would be in ACRIS), first join the ACRIS Real Property Master and ACRIS Real Property Legals datasets by Document ID and Good Through Date. Next select those records from this join where the Doc. Type is either RPTT or RPTT&RET and where Property Type is either SP or SA. The Doc. Type codes are explained in the ACRIS Document Control Codes dataset and the Property Types are explained in the ACRIS Property Types Codes dataset. The NYC Real Property Transfer Tax total consideration will then be the Doc. Amount which is used as the basis for the NYC Real Property Transfer Tax computation. We do not publish the actual tax amount which results from this computation in Open Data. Regards, DOF

requests.request: hi,I want to know these data: Population by census tract,employees，land use divide by community district, https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Community-Districts/yfnk-k7r4 if you can , i want to divide community district by 200meter *200meter cube ,I want to know data in these cube Thank you very much.
requests.response: Hi , I would not suggest aggregating and dividing any census information into arbitrary districts or geometries. You would end up splitting census tracts and then would have to estimate how to reassign split population to each new cube. For example, if one of your cubes splits a census tract by 80% and that tract has 10,000 people - you would most likely assign 80% (8,000 people) to that cube, but in reality, only 2,000 people might actually live in that split up portion. I would suggest using City Planning's Neighborhood Tabulation Area's (NTAs). NTAs are small geographic areas that were created by the New York City Department of City Planning, using whole census tracts from the 2010 Census as building blocks. Each NTA’s boundaries are consistent with Public Use Microdata Areas (PUMAs), approximations of New York City's Community Districts developed for use with the Census Bureau's Public Use Microdata Samples (PUMS). You could then divide population by NTA without splitting census tracts and the data will virtually align to Community Districts (with slight variance). Data Access: NTA boundaries: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Neig... Census Demographics at NTA level: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Cens... Demographic Profiles by PUMA boundaries: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/City-Government/Demo... PUMA boundaries: https://data.cityofnewyork.us/Housing-Development/... For land use information use MapPLUTO: https://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/data-maps/open-... The lots can be split up by NTA and re-aggregated to get percentage of uses in each NTA. Use the Land Use field. To find out the meaning of each Land Use value use the the PLUTO data dictionary (page 21): https://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/... Thank you, - Department of City Planning

requests.response: Hi, Here's what you can find that can help partially meet your needs: DOB Job Application Filings provides construction permit application data for every building that has filed for a permit in approximately the last 10 years. This is not every building in the city. You can get number of Proposed Dwelling Units and number of Proposed Stories (floors). This data is only required on larger construction jobs, so many of the applications will not have values in these fields. DCP has MapPLUTO that offers most of that info for Tax Lots, but for tax lots that contain multiple buildings it is either aggregated (i.e. # of units) or only the primary building info is displayed (i.e. building class). DOITT GIS maintains the Building Footprints and can be joined to DCP MapPLUTO but the issue will remain for lots with multiple buildings. (this probably affects 20% of lots - rough estimate). DOF has Property Assessment data, which includes building classifications (types). Between all of those datasets, you should be able to get the information you're looking for on the majority of buildings in New York City. Thank you, - NYC Department of Buildings (DOB)

For information requests (documents, correspondence, etc.) we encourage you to submit a FOIL request via Open Records: https://a860-openrecords.nyc.gov/ FOIL stands for the Freedom of Information Law. The New York State Freedom of Information Law requires government agencies to provide records to the public upon request. requests.request: I would like data on reported cases of Legionnaire's Disease in the City. A 2014 study by the Department of Health and Mental Hygiene references such data including information on: (1) sex, (2) age, (3) race/ethnicity, (4) pre-existing medical conditions, (5) occupation, (6) nights away from home, (7) recreational water exposures, (8) other risk factors for acquiring Legionella, (9) death. In addition to the information mentioned in the study, it would be helpful if, for each case, information on the (a) date and time of legionellosis positive test result, (b) source of Legionella, (c) any linked cases of Legionella, and (d) location information about where the patients lived at the lowest aggregate level deemed necessary to protect the patients' privacy. I am working on a project to explain some of the recently developed concepts in fair machine learning. One of our goals is to help the public understand some of the fairness issues the City is grappling with as the Automated Decision System Task Force works on its report. The requested data can help answer the family of questions: How do the different fair machine learning techniques compare to each other in predicting risk of Legionnaires’ disease and to the traditional fairness-blind approaches? And in particular, how do their predictions compare when disaggregated into groups based on race and risk factors associated with Legionnaires’ disease such as age and occupation. Thanks to the City’s impressive open data ecosystem, we can conduct several similar and complementary analyses. The Legionnaires’ disease data would allow us to add another layer of nuance adding further value for our audience. Thank you!
requests.response: Thank you for your inquiry about NYC DOHMH communicable disease data, which is not public data pursuant to New York State law. In order to access the data, therefore, you would need to go through the DOHMH data use agreement and IRB processes, which can take time and may not meet the timeline you have set for your work. To begin this process, you may contact Dr. Robert Fitzhenry of the Bureau of Communicable Disease at rfitzhenry@health.nyc.gov to discuss your data needs and the study question(s)you wish to address. Thank you DOHMH

requests.request: Currently, to get to records of the After-Hours Variances permits that the DOB issues, individuals need to know the address of a building and enter it into the DOB’s BISweb. At the bottom right hand side of the resulting page, there is a link to the After-Hours Variances issued for the property. The DOB publishes several datasets that document construction applications and awarded permits on the City’s Open Data Portal, but these datasets do not include AHV permits. Based on our research in collaboration with NYC community boards, we have learned the potential benefits of publishing AHV data online, in a machine-readable format, and updating it daily. We are hoping that the dataset can list every record for an issued AHV application, along with the status of the application, and the BIN of the building under consideration. It would also be great for it to include the responses to certain application questions such as the reason the AHV is being applied for and issued, the number of days applied for and awarded, and whether or not the building is within 200 feet of a residence, involves a demolition, is taking place in an enclosed building, or involves the use of a crane. This is all information that can be accessed on BISweb. We have heard the community boards would like to be able to query 1) the saturation of AHVs being awarded in their districts over time, 2) the number of days AHVs have been awarded at certain buildings, 3) the businesses applying for AHVs, 4) the reasons AHVs are being awarded, and 5) how applicants are responding to the question about whether the site is within 200 ft of a residence.
requests.response: Hi, We are in the process of updating our systems and migrating all of our paper forms online into a new system called DOB NOW. We anticipate releasing data about these permits when they have been added to that new system. We are continuing to roll out new work and permit types, and we suggest you follow our newsletter for updates. Thank you, - NYC Department of Buildings (DOB)

requests.request: NYC Zoning Tax Lot Database Historical from about 2000-present Hi, I am a PhD student at UNC working in conjunction with NYU CUSP. requests.request: To whom it may concern, I hope this e-mail finds you well. I have to come up with a research supported by data. I am writing to you as I would really like to do my research paper on how the presence of places of worship influences social cohesion in New York City (in line with Putnam’s argument). However, I am having a hard time finding datasets on the topic. Do you know if one exists, and if so, where I could find it? Thank you so much for your understanding and your help. how does the presence of places of worship influence social cohesion in New York City?
requests.response: Hello, The data you've requested can be found here: http://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/data-maps/open-d... You can use either PLUTO or MapPLUTO. The differences between them are; 1) MapPLUTO is a spatial dataset while PLUTO is tabular, 2) MapPLUTO is released as 5 separate shapefiles (1 for each Borough) while PLUTO has the entire City combined To find tax lots (or parcels) containing houses of worship, you need to filter the data using the 'Building Class' field. Any lot that starts with "M" is a house of worship. You can further filter them down by specific types of house of worship: M. CHURCHES, SYNAGOGUES, ETC. 1. Church, Synagogue, Chapel 2. Mission House (Non-Residential) 3. Parsonage, Rectory 4. Convents 9. Miscellaneous (note: church = M1, parsonage = M3, convent = M4, etc.) If you have additional questions regarding PLUTO/MapPLUTO please consult the data dictionary which can will answer most of your questions: http://www1.nyc.gov/assets/planning/download/pdf/d... Thank you, - NYC Open Data

In the meantime, you may be interested in the 2010 Landcover Rasters and the Urban Tree Canopy Assessment Metrics datasets currently on the portal (links below). requests.request: Hello New York Preservations and Landmarks Committee, I am working on a data science research project for my degree in Architectural History that requires me to access information about New York City landmarks. I see however that the construction years are available from this map created by the Landmarks Preservation Committe on the ArcGIS platform: https://www.arcgis.com/home/webmap/viewer.html?webmap=a38d198df9bc469a8b452d416dd90328 I am not an ArcGIS user, and I do not know how to extract the data from this map as an excel or CSV file of building names, dates, etc. I was wondering if you could possibly send me this information as a spreadsheet or update the information on your open data website to include each building's year of construction. requests.response: Dear, Apologies for the delay in answering your question, we had a technical glitch in receiving it. requests.request: Zoning lists with addresses not just block and lots. and size of lots want to do a mass search of addresses
requests.response: Hi, Currently there is not a dataset that lists every single address and with the zoning. However, there are several applications you can use to determine the zoning for every known address: 1) ZOLA: You can search for zoning by address using NYC Department of City Planning's Zola application: https://zola.planning.nyc.gov/about#9.72/40.7125/-... 2) PLUTO: NYC Department of City Planning also releases PLUTO & MapPLUTO datasets. This dataset has the zoning, commercial overlay and special district for each lot in the city. For most lots, a single address is also listed so you could try searching or filtering for that address within PLUTO to see the zoning. Download PLUTO: http://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/data-maps/open-d... 3) GOAT/GBAT: If you know an address but do not know the lot (or vice versa), you can use the GOAT application for single queries or GBAT for batch queries. GOAT: http://a030-goat.nyc.gov/goat/Default.aspx use the Address tab if you know an address and want Borough/Block/Lot (BBL) number use the Block & Lot tab if you know the Borough/Block/Lot (BBL) number and want an address GBAT/Geosupport Desktop Edition: http://www1.nyc.gov/site/planning/data-maps/open-d... Thank you, - NYC Open Data

requests.request: I'd like for NYC to open the Public Access Defibrillation registry, which is held by the Fire Department of New York and/or New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene in coordination with NYC's Regional Emergency Medical Services Council (NYC REMSCO). Context and details: There are various programs in New York City & New York State either encouraging or requiring buildings/businesses/locations to have automated external defibrillators (AEDs) available for public use. New York state law & NYC law applies; also see NYC local law 20 - mandated, and New York City Administrative Code § 17-188. Per the New York State Department of Health advisory on Public Access Defibrillation at https://www.health.ny.gov/professionals/ems/policy/09-03.htm , each regional emergency medical services council holds a PAD registry. In New York City, that is NYC REMSCO http://www.nycremsco.org/bcls.asp?intCategoryID=10&intArticleID=329 . The REMSCO shares this with 911 operators, who, in case of cardiac arrest, can advise callers if there's a PAD at the address they're calling from. The last publicly published map of PAD locations in New York City was in 2006 http://www.nyc.gov/html/records/pdf/govpub/2498reportonlocallaw20july2006final.pdf . Per that report, NYC REMSCO has "an online registration system intended to facilitate registration, reduce paperwork, and improve the scope and accuracy of future reporting to City Council", and this was developed in coordination with New York City Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH). The Fire Department of NY advertises a Be 911 app http://www1.nyc.gov/site/fdny/about/resources/mobile-applications/fdny-be-911-life-saver-app.page which accesses NYC's PAD registry and tells the user of 3 AEDs near the user's location. Thus we know that this dataset is available, machine-readable, and regularly updated, and that at least part of the stewardship of this dataset is through the Fire Department. Per NYC REMSCO's "Elements of a Successful and Compliant PAD Program" http://www.nycremsco.org/images/articlesserver/01-Elements%20of%20a%20Successful%20and%20Compliant%20PAD%20Program.pdf , the PAD registry includes data from the following forms: * Notice of Intent to Provide Public Access Defibrillation * PAD Provider Information Form * Collaborative Agreement * Quality Assurance Report I want to know where public access defibrillators are in New York City so I can raise awareness among local health advocates. The PAD registry dataset includes, for instance, the street addresses of buildings with AEDs, the "agency" type ("agencies" including "Physician's Office", "Transportation Hub" "Stadium", "Business" and other categories), and the number of trained providers and AED units at each location. With that data, I would be able to: * remix AED locations into other mapping applications * create a map of AEDs in my area * map out "AED deserts" and donate AEDs to local nonprofits in those neighborhoods, or tell local merchants' associations that there's a tax credit for buying an AED https://www.tax.ny.gov/pit/credits/defibrillator_credit.htm ("The credit is equal to the purchase cost of the unit, or $500, whichever is less.")
requests.response: FDNY does not maintain PAD's (Public Access Defibrillation) database. It is managed by The Regional Emergency Medical Services Council of New York City (REMSCO).

requests.request: Post Vaccination Evaluation of Anti HBsAg Antibody Titers among Haemodialysis Patients - Hepatitis B virus (HBV) is the second most common viral infection which poses threat of infection among health care workers and those individuals treated for various debilitated conditions in hospital settings. Patients undergoing haemodialysis are at a greater risk of acquiring HBV infection. Although HBV vaccination has been in use for almost three decades, it is not completely certain about its efficacy in long-term protection. Few studies in the past have emphasized the need for evaluation of anti-HBsAg antibody titers among high risk groups that include patients undergoing haemodialysis. Studies in the past have also noted that few vaccinated group do not respond to HBV vaccine and that few other group of vaccinated individuals develop inadequate antibody titers. The present study evaluated the antibody titers among haemodialysis patients and health care workers.
requests.response: If you are still interested, please submit a new request for specific data. -NYC Open Data Team

requests.request: Zinc deficiency induces apoptosis via mitochondrial p53- and caspase-dependent pathways in human neuronal precursor cells - Previous studies have shown that zinc deficiency leads to apoptosis of neuronal precursor cells in vivo and in vitro. In addition to the role of p53 as a nuclear transcription factor in zinc deficient cultured human neuronal precursors (NT-2), we have now identified the translocation of phosphorylated p53 to the mitochondria and p53-dependent increases in the pro-apoptotic mitochondrial protein BAX leading to a loss of mitochondrial membrane potential as demonstrated by a 25% decrease in JC-1 red:green fluorescence ratio. Disruption of mitochondrial membrane integrity was accompanied by efflux of the apoptosis inducing factor (AIF) from the mitochondria and translocation to the nucleus with a significant increase in reactive oxygen species (ROS) after 24 h of zinc deficiency. Measurement of caspase cleavage, mRNA, and treatment with caspase inhibitors revealed the involvement of caspases 2, 3, 6, and 7 in zinc deficiency-mediated apoptosis. Down-stream targets of caspase activation, including the nuclear structure protein lamin and polyADP ribose polymerase (PARP), which participates in DNA repair, were also cleaved. Transfection with a dominant-negative p53 construct and use of the p53 inhibitor, pifithrin- è‰¶ï½¨, established that these alterations were largely dependent on p53. Together these data identify a cascade of events involving mitochondrial p53 as well as p53-dependent caspase-mediated mechanisms leading to apoptosis during zinc deficiency.

requests.agency: Department of Health and Mental Hygiene (DOHMH)
requests.request: Indices to NYC vital records (i.e. birth index, death index, etc.) - I was to make a formal request for these datasets here, as a follow-up up to a Twitter and e-mail conversation I had with her recently. I am requesting that the city publish its vital records indices online as open data. Please note that this is not a request for any actual certificate information, which of course have strict privacy rules, but merely the indices to the basic data. These data sets, which are held by the New York City Department of Health, have been previously published in other (older) forms, although all are incomplete. For example, the city birth index from 1881-1965 is available as microfilm images at Family History Libraries across the world, and the city death index through 1982 or 1983 is available in a tiny number of libraries in printed book form. Agreeing that the indices are public data, the New York State (not city) Department of Health has recently begun adding their State death index data to their Socrata portal for the years 1957-1962. It would be nice to see the city follow suit. Here are the data sets that would be helpful: 1) Index of all births reported in the city of New York, 1881 (or as early as data is available) through 2012 (or as recently as data is available) Fields in this dataset should include, at a minimum: - first name - surname - gender - date of birth (or year, if date is unavailable) - borough of birth - certificate number 2) Index of all deaths reported in the city of New York, 1881 (or as early as data is available) through 2012 (or as recently as data is available) Fields in this dataset should include, at a minimum: - first name - surname - gender - date of death (or year, if date is unavailable) - borough of death - certificate number 3) Index of all marriages reported in the city of New York, 1881 (or as early as data is available) through 2012 (or as recently as data is available) Fields in this dataset should include, at a minimum: - first name of bride (or spouse #1) - surname of bride (or spouse #1) - gender of of bride (or spouse #1) - date of birth (or year, if date is unavailable) of bride (or spouse #1) - first name of groom (or spouse #2) - surname of groom (or spouse #2) - gender of of groom (or spouse #2) - date of birth (or year, if date is unavailable) of groom (or spouse #2) - date of marriage (or date of issuance of marriage license) - borough where marriage took place - certificate number 4) Index of all domestic partnerships reported in the city of New York, 1997 through 2012 (or as recently as data is available) Fields in this dataset should include, at a minimum: - first name of partner #1 - surname of partner #1 - gender of of partner #1 - date of birth (or year, if date is unavailable) of partner #1 - first name of partner #2 - surname of partner #2 - gender of of partner #2 - date of birth (or year, if date is unavailable) of partner #2 - date of issuance of partnership certificate - borough of residence of the partners - certificate number For the index to divorce decrees and/or certificates, you will probably have to direct this request to each individual borough in the city, to their courts, not to the city's Department of Health: 5) Index of all divorces reported in the city of New York, 1881 (or as early as data is available) through 2012 (or as recently as data is available) Fields in this dataset should include, at a minimum: - first name of bride (or spouse #1) - surname of bride (or spouse #1) - gender of of bride (or spouse #1) - date of birth (or year, if date is unavailable) of bride (or spouse #1) - first name of groom (or spouse #2) - surname of groom (or spouse #2) - gender of of groom (or spouse #2) - date of birth (or year, if date is unavailable) of groom (or spouse #2) - date of divorce decree or certificate - borough where divorce took place - certificate number or decree number I anticipate that the NYC Department of Health may try to claim to you that these indices are private or protected data, but as I mentioned in my initial request e-mails, this is clearly not the case. The certificates are private, yes, but the indices are not private, are not copyrighted, and have been published in other forms previously. Please let me know if there is any other information you'd like me to provide regarding this request. Thanks.
requests.response: Section 558(c) of the Charter requires the NYC Board of Health to include in the NYC Health Code provisions related to maintaining a registry of births and deaths. Section 556(c)(1) of the Charter authorizes the NYC Department of Health and Mental Hygiene to supervise and control the registration of births and deaths. Section 17-170 of the New York City Administrative Code authorizes the Board to determine when birth and death records are transferred to DORIS. Administrative Code section 17-169 and Health Code sections 3.25 and 207.11 make birth and death records confidential and restrict access to these records beyond certain classes of specified people. Section 17-170(b) of the Administrative Code authorizes the Board to determine when birth and death records are transferred to DORIS. In 2008, the Board of Health specifically repealed the Health Code provision that permitted public access to the vital records index books. Please see attached, pages 4 – 5.

requests.request: I clicked on the download option:
requests.response: The local law defines data as final versions of statistical or factual information (1) in alphanumeric form reflected in a list, table, graph, chart or other non-narrative form, that can be digitally transmitted or processed; and (2) regularly created or maintained by or on behalf of and owned by an agency that records a measurement, transaction, or determination related to the mission of an agency. Such term shall not include information provided to an agency by other governmental entities, nor shall it include image files, such as designs, drawings, maps, photos, or scanned copies of original documents, provided that it shall include statistical or factual information about such image files and shall include geographic information system data. The Zoning Resolution is a set of regulations - it is not a data set. To try to distill zoning regulations into a table or even a series of tables is overly reductive and not an accurate representation of the law. The table that you refer to that is available from DCPs website is an extract from the Zoning Handbook, last published in 2011. While the Handbook is a helpful guide, it is just that, and there's a context for its utility. DCP does not regularly create or maintain such tables, and data, per the definition, is required to be regularly created or maintained and excludes image files and copies of original documents. We will likely have to update the Handbook tables in the near future, since the Zoning for Quality and Affordability zoning text amendment was adopted by the City Council on March 22nd and represents one of the most comprehensive changes to the ZR in decades. That said, we would not update them on a regular basis going forward to reflect every nuance of zoning that changes. That is why referring people to the ZR itself is the "safest" and most accurate thing to do. We don't disagree that these tables are useful and helpful, but we do not believe they belong in Open Data. While they represent the framework of zoning, we do not want to overemphasize or mischaracterize their utility. Moreover, there are various tables within the Zoning Resolution, and we would not want to confuse the public with additional tables that look like the legal tables but which are not.
